source_text: Videamus ergo, quomodo huc redeat etiam pars tuae secunda sententiae. Dixisti enim: Qui dicit naturam humanam bonum non esse, bonum negat conditae Creatorem; qui vero negat ei malum inesse, misericordem vitiatae invidet Salvatorem [n257] . Si ergo, ut tu profiteri coactus es, qui negat eam bonum esse, bonum etiam Conditorem eius id est Deum negat, et nihil aliud est malam esse naturam quam malum meritum habere naturaliter; veritati nostrae amminiculatur etiam vestra confessio negare vos videlicet Deum bonum hominum conditorem, quorum malam esse naturam et vitiis eius iuratis et poenis.
pass_a_gloss: Let us see therefore how here also the second part of your sentence returns. For you have said: Who says human nature is not a good denies a good Creator of the founded; but who denies evil is in it begrudges a merciful Savior to the vitiated. If therefore, as you have been forced to profess, who denies it is a good also denies its good Founder, that is God, and nothing other is for nature to be evil than to have evil desert naturally; even your confession assists our truth, namely that you deny God the good founder of humans, whose nature you swear is evil both by its vices and by punishments.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS meritum; Blaise; avoid later merit-theology

pass_b_english: Let us see, then, how the second part of your statement returns to this point too. You said: ‘Whoever says human nature is not good denies a good Creator to the nature created; whoever denies it contains evil begrudges a merciful Savior to the nature corrupted’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36). As you have been forced to profess, anyone denying that it is good also denies its good Creator, that is, God. And for nature to be evil means nothing other than to possess evil desert naturally. Thus even your confession supports our truth: you deny the good God as creator of humans, whose nature you swear is evil, appealing both to its vices and to its punishments.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's ethnic-rhetorical slur for Augustine; keep the geographic sting rather than neutralizing it.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
